description:
I’m leaning toward the “Flame in Free Fall” challenge and will compete at the Hanoi local event. I’m happy to connect with other participants to exchange ideas, feedback or resources during the event.

Skills: rapid prototyping, data analysis, AI/LLM-assisted development, web and app development, and turning research into a working demo.
summary:
EMBER is a web dashboard that shows what NASA’s microgravity fire experiments say will happen in any closed place where people breathe, and where nobody has tested yet. We cleaned 1,169 runs from 8 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics combustion investigations and plotted each one by oxygen and pressure. A machine-learning model draws the “burns or goes out” boundary only where tested runs support it, and shows “No evidence here” elsewhere. Every answer is cited to a NASA source passage.

For Flame in Freefall, EMBER turns scattered NASA tables into a clear, honest safety reference. Pick the Moon habitat and the map shows zero solid-material runs and zero lunar-gravity runs in the data, which is the gap future missions must fill. The same map covers Earth settings with oxygen-rich air or limited airflow, such as hospital oxygen wards, hyperbaric chambers and airliner cabins, and links NASA fire research to technology we use today.

It matters because agencies are planning oxygen-rich, low-pressure habitats. Designers and students need to see what the evidence proves and what it doesn’t, without a made-up safety score.
details:
What it does. EMBER is a web dashboard that answers one question for any closed place where people breathe: what does NASA’s microgravity combustion evidence say fire will do here, and what has nobody tested yet? You pick a place (Moon habitat, rover, ISS, hospital oxygen ward, hyperbaric chamber, airliner cabin) and a material.

How it works.

  1. Evidence map. We cleaned 1,169 runs from 8 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion investigations. Each run is plotted by oxygen % against pressure. Missing values stay null, and assumed values are drawn as hollow dots.
  2. Flammability boundary. We trained models (logistic regression for droplets and gas, gradient-boosted trees for solids) on 502 labelled 0 g runs. They were scored by leaving out whole test days. Pooled balanced accuracy is 0.746, against 0.671 for an oxygen-only baseline. The gas model does not beat that baseline (0.680 vs 0.688), so it is labelled “experiment”. Wherever fewer than a minimum number of tested runs are nearby, the map shows “No evidence here” and draws no line.
  3. Ranked gaps. The app lists the nearest NASA studies and what is missing. For the Moon habitat (8.2 psia, 34% O₂, ⅙ g) the cleaned data has zero solid-material runs and zero lunar-gravity runs.
  4. Cited answers. Every sentence comes from 103 verified passages. In our audit, 62 of 62 cited sentences traced to a source, and 5 of 5 out-of-scope questions were refused.
  5. Same map for Earth. Evidence cards cover oxygen-rich medicine, smoke in low-ventilation spaces and aircraft cabins. The spinoff trail covers the water-mist extinguisher, the air-sampling fire detector, firefighter air tanks and protective clothing.

Benefits and impact. Habitat designers, safety engineers and students get an honest starting reference, not a “safety score”. The Moon-gap finding shows where the next experiments are needed (NASA’s planned FM2 and LUCI). The Earth view connects the same physics to fires that kill people today, including oxygen-therapy and apartment-building fires.

Tools. Python (pandas and scikit-learn) for data cleaning and the ML, TypeScript, React and Vite for the app, and Three.js for the 3D views. The app is static-first, so it works signed-out with no backend. Cached answers are the default, and a live question box is an optional extra. We also published the cleaned dataset on Kaggle.

Creativity. Most dashboards smooth over sparse data. EMBER treats refusing to extrapolate as a feature, in both the ML map and the Q&A. Interactive 3D hardware (a BASS-II chamber cutaway, habitats, suits, extinguishers) anchors the abstract axes in real equipment.

What we considered.

  • No false transfer. We never claim microgravity results hold on the Moon or on Earth.
  • Labels. Solid outcomes were labelled with SI from NASA’s report. A human check of 20 of the 113 labels agreed on all 20.
  • Pressure. Pressure for those solid runs is assumed at 101.3 kPa and marked as such.
  • Disclosure. All SI use and every third-party source is disclosed. SI-generated 3D models carry an on-screen label. NASA data is credited (CC0 where PSI states it).
